title: Spain Lifts the Trophy, But the 2026 World Cup Leaves Big Questions
summary:
The 2026 FIFA World Cup — the largest in history — concluded with Spain hoisting the trophy after a decisive victory over Argentina. But as the confetti settles, the tournament has left behind a tangle of debates: Should the World Cup expand to 64 teams? Were the hydration breaks necessary? And how much did the U.S.–Iran conflict shape the event?

On the pitch, the expanded 48-team format was a surprising success. Critics had warned it would dilute the quality, but instead it delivered some of the tournament's most memorable moments. Debutants Cape Verde, a squad of journeymen and raw youngsters, captured hearts by holding Spain and Uruguay to draws and forcing Argentina into extra time. Their run proved that the gap between traditional powerhouses and emerging nations is shrinking. For the finalists, the expansion meant only one extra match — a small price for the global growth FIFA insists it funds through World Cup revenue.

Yet the expansion wasn't without friction. The additional teams stretched the tournament's length, and the introduction of hydration breaks — mandated due to heat — drew loud boos from stadium crowds. Fans argued that the stoppages disrupted the rhythm of the game, turning fluid 45-minute halves into choppy segments. FIFA defended the breaks as a player safety measure, but the backlash was unmistakable.

Off the field, geopolitics loomed large. The U.S., a co-host, was engaged in a joint military operation with Israel against Iran, a competing nation. A last-minute ceasefire allowed the tournament to proceed, but visa issues plagued the Iranian contingent and fans from several countries. Hostilities resumed after Iran's group-stage exit, casting a shadow over the event. The situation highlighted the increasingly blurred line between sport and global politics.

Looking ahead, FIFA is already floating a 64-team format for 2030. Under that model, only the top two from each of 16 groups would advance, meaning finalists would play no extra games. Nations like Italy, Nigeria, and Cameroon — who have missed recent tournaments — would likely welcome the change. But as the 2026 edition showed, more isn't always better. The question now is whether the beautiful game can keep its soul as it grows.
why_it_matters: This tournament shows how global sports events are not just about the game; they can become arenas for political disputes and test the limits of growth versus quality, raising questions about what fans value most — and how their money and attention shape the future of football.

background_read: FIFA, the global governing body of football, has gradually expanded the World Cup over the years, from 13 teams in 1930 to 32 in 1998 and 48 for the 2026 tournament.
Cape Verde, a small island nation off the coast of West Africa with a population of about 600,000, had never before qualified for the World Cup finals.

The United States and Iran have been adversaries for decades, with military clashes occasionally flaring — for example, the 2020 U.S. drone strike that killed an Iranian general. Israel and Iran are also regional rivals, and Israel has carried out airstrikes on Iranian targets in Syria.

In international sports, politics often seeps into the event: past World Cups have seen boycotts, protests, and tensions spill onto the pitch, showing that the line between sport and global affairs is never completely solid.

perspectives.description: Fans of smaller football nations and FIFA itself argue that expansion brings more countries into the spotlight, boosting global interest and funding for grassroots development.

Critics, including many traditional fans, say the expanded tournament waters down the competition, creates fixture congestion, and forces players to suffer in extreme heat with disruptive breaks that spoil the spectacle.

Observers note that the real-world conflicts around the event highlight the deep connection between international sports and politics — a pattern seen in past boycotts and protests, where athletes and fans become pawns in larger disputes.

Looking ahead, the debate over a 64-team World Cup will force a choice between commercial growth and preserving the quality and spontaneity that made the game beloved — and players may need stronger voices in such decisions.
